title: Cardiovascular Physiology
subtitle: Cardiac function, circulation, ECG and blood physiology
scope: Physiology-only selection from the existing Cardiovascular System review. The 27 original physiology and blood sections are preserved with their figures, self-checks and source references. Anatomy, histology, embryology, mixed appendices and transcript attachments are excluded.

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Depolarization travels down T tubules, opens L-type calcium channels and triggers ryanodine receptor-mediated calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium binds troponin C, permitting actin-myosin cycling. Relaxation requires SERCA reuptake, sodium-calcium exchange and extrusion. ATP is required both for cross-bridge cycling and restoration of calcium gradients. The long action potential/refractory period prevents fused tetanic contraction and preserves filling intervals.

Beta-1 stimulation increases cAMP-dependent calcium handling and pacemaker activity, raising contractility and rate while accelerating relaxation. Parasympathetic M2 signaling reduces cAMP and increases potassium conductance, slowing nodal firing/conduction. Do not repeat ASR phrases that swap sympathetic with parasympathetic or call outward K+ current an influx.

blocks.question: Why does increased extracellular calcium availability affect cardiac contraction more directly than ordinary skeletal contraction?
blocks.answer: Cardiac excitation-contraction coupling depends on calcium entry through L-type channels to trigger SR release. Skeletal muscle uses mechanically coupled voltage sensors and SR release much more directly. Cardiac force therefore depends strongly on the extracellular trigger calcium.

sections.title: Pacemakers, AV delay and conduction failure

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: The SA node normally dominates because its spontaneous depolarization reaches threshold faster than other latent pacemakers. Impulses spread through atria, slow in AV nodal tissue, then traverse His bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje network to activate ventricular myocardium rapidly. AV delay permits atrial contraction to precede ventricular contraction. Purkinje conduction is rapid; AV nodal conduction is relatively slow. The fibrous AV separation forces the normal impulse through this specialized connection.

An ectopic focus or re-entry circuit can compete with the sinus node. Re-entry requires an excitable pathway, unidirectional block and a conduction delay sufficient for tissue ahead to recover excitability. A premature ventricular beat can produce a wide QRS because activation spreads abnormally through ventricular myocardium rather than rapidly through the normal network. AV nodal blockade can expose a slower escape rhythm from subsidiary pacemakers.

blocks.title: Electrical versus mechanical
blocks.text: A recorded depolarization does not prove an effective pulse. Electrical activation must still generate coordinated calcium-dependent contraction, fill the chamber and eject against the outflow pressure.

sections.title: Cardiac cycle, pressure crossings and heart sounds

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Valve motion follows pressure gradients. At the start of ventricular systole, ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure and AV valves close. During isovolumetric contraction both inlet and outlet valves of that ventricle are closed, pressure rises and volume remains at EDV. When ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, the semilunar valve opens and ejection begins. At the end of ejection, arterial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure and the semilunar valve closes. Isovolumetric relaxation reduces pressure at ESV until atrial pressure opens the AV valve.

rows: After P wave; augments ventricular filling
S1; atrial c wave partly from AV valve bulging
Near end of T wave/mechanical systole

blocks.text: P represents atrial depolarization, not atrial contraction itself. QRS precedes ventricular pressure rise, and T reflects ventricular repolarization. At faster rates diastole shortens disproportionately, reducing filling time and coronary perfusion time. Right and left heart valves do not all change state at exactly the same instant. Inspiration normally delays pulmonary closure relative to aortic closure, producing physiologic S2 splitting.

blocks.question: What happens to ventricular volume between mitral closure and aortic opening?
blocks.answer: It remains approximately constant at EDV while pressure rises. The interval is isovolumetric contraction. If an inlet or outlet valve is incompetent, the ideal truly isovolumetric assumption no longer applies.

sections.title: Pressure-volume loops, preload, afterload and contractility

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Stroke volume is EDV minus ESV, and ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by EDV. A normal teaching example of EDV 120 mL and ESV 50 mL gives SV 70 mL and EF about 58%. Cardiac output is HR times SV, so 70 beats/min times 70 mL is 4.9 L/min. These numbers are illustrative, not universal individual reference intervals. A PV loop is traced counterclockwise: filling, isovolumetric contraction, ejection and isovolumetric relaxation.

rows: More initial fiber stretch increases force through Frank-Starling behavior
Higher systolic pressure, greater ESV and smaller SV initially
More pressure required before and during ejection
Lower ESV, steeper end-systolic relation and greater SV
More force at a given preload
Higher filling pressure for a given EDV
Stiffer chamber shifts diastolic pressure-volume relation upward

blocks.text: Preload describes initial myocardial stretch and is approximated by end-diastolic volume/pressure only in context. Afterload is wall stress opposing shortening, not simply blood pressure in every situation. Contractility is intrinsic force generation at a given loading condition, not increased force merely because preload rose. The loop area represents external stroke work. Pressure development and wall tension also consume oxygen even when ejected volume is limited.

blocks.caption: Work through the valve events at each corner before interpreting changes in loop width or height.

blocks.question: A ventricle has a normal EF but requires an abnormally high filling pressure to reach its EDV. Which property is impaired?
blocks.answer: Diastolic compliance is reduced. EF alone does not measure ease of filling and cannot exclude dysfunction in a stiff ventricle.

sections.title: Pressure, flow, resistance and vascular networks

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Flow Q equals pressure difference divided by resistance: Q = (Pin - Pout)/R. A high absolute pressure does not imply high flow if downstream pressure rises equally. For systemic circulation, the driving difference is approximately MAP minus right atrial pressure. Pulmonary resistance uses mean pulmonary arterial minus left atrial/wedge pressure, divided by pulmonary flow. Always keep units consistent: pressure in mmHg and flow in L/min yield mmHg·min/L, not the older mmHg·s/mL resistance unit.

For an ideal rigid cylindrical tube with steady laminar Newtonian flow, resistance is 8ηL/(πr^4). Doubling radius reduces resistance to one-sixteenth if other factors remain unchanged. Halving radius raises resistance sixteenfold. Real blood is non-Newtonian and vessels are compliant/branching/pulsatile, so this law is a model rather than an exact description of every vessel. Hematocrit strongly affects viscosity. Plasma proteins also contribute. Values depend on temperature and shear rate.

rows: Same steady flow passes sequential components; pressure drops add
Branches share an inlet-outlet pressure difference; flows add
Average right and left output are equal at steady state
Each organ regulates its own resistance and share of output

blocks.question: Three equal vascular beds of resistance 6 units are perfused in parallel. What is total resistance, and what happens if one closes?
blocks.answer: Initially 1/R = 3/6, giving R = 2 units. With two open beds R = 3 units. At an unchanged pressure difference, total flow falls to two-thirds of the initial value. Flow through each remaining bed need not fall if its own resistance and driving pressure remain unchanged.

blocks.text: In a thin-walled cylindrical vessel, circumferential tension per unit length is approximately transmural pressure times radius, and wall stress is approximately pressure times radius divided by wall thickness. A thin spherical chamber has a factor of two in the corresponding denominator. These geometric idealizations explain why dilation raises required tension and why thicker walls can reduce stress; tension, stress and pressure are not interchangeable quantities. Compliance is absolute volume change per pressure change, while distensibility divides that volume change by starting volume. The arterial-pressure section applies the distinction to pulse pressure.

sections.title: Velocity, Bernoulli, Reynolds and flow measurement

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Average velocity equals flow divided by total cross-sectional area, v = Q/A. Capillary velocity is low because the many parallel capillaries have a very large aggregate area. A small single vessel does not necessarily have slower velocity if the same flow is forced through it. Across a narrowed segment at fixed flow, velocity rises. By contrast, when pressure gradient is fixed and a tube narrows, resistance rises and flow falls. The held-constant condition determines the correct answer.

Reynolds number is proportional to density × velocity × diameter / viscosity. Higher Reynolds numbers favor turbulence. Rapid flow, large diameter and low viscosity can increase the tendency. A stenosis promotes disturbances through high local velocity and geometry despite its reduced diameter. The lecture inequalities on laminar/turbulent flow are reversed: turbulence is associated with higher, not lower, Reynolds number. Thresholds in pulsatile branching vessels are not one universal hard boundary.

Bernoulli relates static pressure, kinetic energy per volume and gravitational potential for ideal flow along a streamline. Higher velocity can accompany lower local static pressure, but real vascular flow also loses energy through viscous resistance. Hydrostatic pressure is ρgh relative to a reference level. Mean systemic filling pressure is a volume/tone-dependent pressure when flow ceases, not simply another name for ρgh. Pulse-wave speed is propagation of a pressure disturbance and differs from the actual velocity of blood.

items: An electromagnetic flowmeter detects voltage generated by conductive fluid moving across a magnetic field; direction depends on the geometry of field, flow and electrodes.

Doppler estimates velocity from frequency shift and insonation angle. Converting velocity to volume flow also requires a cross-sectional area estimate. An angle near 90 degrees makes axial Doppler sensitivity poor.

blocks.question: Why may anemia increase a flow murmur despite reduced blood viscosity?
blocks.answer: Lower viscosity raises Reynolds number, and compensatory increased cardiac output can raise velocity. Both can favor disturbed/turbulent flow. A murmur does not automatically prove a structurally abnormal valve.

sections.title: Measurement principles and regional circulations

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: A pressure transducer converts deformation into an electrical signal. Calibration, a correctly chosen reference height and a fluid system without major damping/resonance are essential: a precise number is not necessarily an accurate pressure. Electromagnetic flow measurement uses the voltage induced as conductive blood moves through a magnetic field. Doppler estimates velocity from frequency shift; beam angle matters. Volume flow requires velocity and vessel cross-sectional area, so a velocity measurement is not automatically a cardiac-output measurement.

The Fick principle obtains flow from conservation of a transported substance. For oxygen, CO equals oxygen consumption divided by arterial-minus-mixed-venous oxygen content. If oxygen consumption is 250 mL/min and the difference is 5 mL/dL, output is 50 dL/min, or 5 L/min. A pulmonary-artery sample represents mixed systemic venous return better than a random peripheral vein. Indicator-dilution and thermodilution methods infer flow from how a known indicator is diluted over time; recirculation and technique affect interpretation.

blocks.question: Doppler velocity doubles while vessel diameter halves. Does volume flow double?
blocks.answer: No. Area becomes one quarter, and flow equals velocity times area. With uniform mean-velocity assumptions, the resulting flow is one half of the original.

sections.title: Compliance, pulse pressure, MAP and measurement

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Compliance is ΔV/ΔP. Distensibility is fractional volume change per pressure change, ΔV/(VΔP), so compliance equals distensibility times initial volume. Veins are highly compliant volume reservoirs. Arterial elastic recoil sustains diastolic flow after ventricular ejection. Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic pressure and approximately rises with stroke volume and falls with arterial compliance, although ejection speed and wave reflection also matter.

For a resting rate, MAP is often estimated as DBP plus one-third pulse pressure. For 120/80 mmHg this is about 93 mmHg, not 100 exactly. The arithmetic average is wrong because diastole lasts longer. At high heart rates or unusual waveforms, the approximation is less accurate and waveform integration is preferable. Both systolic and diastolic pressures reflect multiple cardiac and vascular factors; they are not isolated tests of heart health versus vessel health.

A cuff above systolic pressure occludes arterial flow. With slow deflation the first Korotkoff sound usually estimates systolic pressure, and disappearance estimates adult diastolic pressure in routine conditions. Palpation alone estimates systolic pressure because it detects reappearance of a pulse, not the transition to silent flow. Cuff size, arm height, rest, movement and deflation speed matter. An arm below heart level produces a hydrostatic overestimate.

blocks.question: Two patients have the same stroke volume but one has much stiffer large arteries. Predict pulse pressure and explain.
blocks.answer: Reduced compliance means the same added volume produces a greater pressure rise, so pulse pressure tends to be wider. This does not require a larger stroke volume. Wave reflection can further augment the difference.

sections.title: Venous return, capacitance, posture and cardiac output

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: At steady state cardiac output equals venous return. Venous return can be modeled as (mean systemic filling pressure - right atrial pressure)/resistance to venous return. Increasing right atrial pressure tends to oppose return if other variables are unchanged, while increasing systemic filling pressure favors return. Venoconstriction recruits blood from an unstressed reservoir into stressed volume and can raise systemic filling pressure. Infusion can also shift the venous return curve, whereas hemorrhage shifts it in the opposite direction.

The actual operating point is the intersection of cardiac-function and venous-return curves. Increased contractility can increase output while lowering right atrial pressure. Pump failure often reduces output and raises right atrial pressure. A very negative right atrial pressure eventually collapses susceptible great veins, limiting further return. More suction does not produce unlimited flow.

Standing adds hydrostatic pressure below the heart and subtracts it above. Venous pooling lowers central blood volume until muscle pump, respiratory pump, venous valves and reflex venoconstriction compensate. The pressure increment depends on vertical height, not whether a person is at sea level. Atrial stretch can trigger Bainbridge tachycardia and promotes natriuretic peptide release and reduced water retention. Frank-Starling is an intrinsic length-force mechanism, not itself the Bainbridge neural reflex.

blocks.question: Why can a failing heart have elevated venous pressure but low forward output?
blocks.answer: High atrial pressure reflects impaired emptying and backward pressure. It also reduces the systemic-to-atrial driving gradient for venous return. Filling pressure and effective output therefore need not move together.

sections.title: Venous-return curves, transmural pressure and feedback timing

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: At a steady operating point cardiac output equals venous return. A cardiac-function curve and a venous-return curve must be solved together. Mean systemic filling pressure is the zero-flow intercept of the return relation; resistance to venous return determines its slope. Increasing resistance flattens the curve without necessarily moving the intercept. Increasing stressed volume or venous tone usually raises the intercept. At very negative right-atrial pressure, collapse of compliant veins creates a plateau, so extrapolating the straight line predicts an impossible unlimited return.

Transmural filling pressure is intracavitary pressure minus surrounding pressure. Raising pressure around the heart by 6 mmHg requires a 6-mmHg rise inside to preserve the same distending pressure. Thus positive-pressure ventilation can raise measured central venous pressure while reducing effective filling and venous return. These effects depend on lung mechanics, blood volume and ventricular function; CVP alone is not a direct measure of preload volume.

Loss of widespread sympathetic tone expands venous capacity and lowers filling pressure generated by the same blood volume. Loss of cardiac sympathetic stimulation may simultaneously lower the cardiac-function curve. A large arteriovenous fistula initially lowers circuit resistance and rotates the return curve upward; later reflex/renal-volume adaptations may raise filling pressure. Immediate resistance effects and later volume effects are distinct. After a transfusion, redistribution and vascular stress-relaxation can partly reverse the initial increase in output.

Baroreceptors buffer rapid variation but partly reset during sustained mechanical pressure change. Electrical afferent stimulation bypasses mechanical transduction and need not reproduce receptor resetting. Low-pressure atrial/vascular stretch signals promote renal volume excretion through neural and hormonal paths. Renal pressure-natriuresis equilibrium occurs where excretion matches intake: changing intake or shifting the excretion curve changes the eventual equilibrium pressure. A volume-driven rise in pressure can later show near-normal output with higher peripheral resistance because tissues autoregulate.

blocks.question: A supplied model has CO = 2 + PRA and VR = 5 - 0.5PRA, with flows in L/min and pressure in mmHg. Where is equilibrium?
blocks.answer: Equate the flows: 2 + PRA = 5 - 0.5PRA. Therefore PRA = 2 mmHg and both flows equal 4 L/min. Neither the heart curve nor the vascular curve alone determines the answer.

blocks.question: Why can a spinal sympathetic block reduce output without blood leaving the circulation?
blocks.answer: Loss of venous tone increases unstressed capacity and reduces mean systemic filling pressure; effective circulating filling is reduced even when total blood volume is unchanged. Concurrent reduction of cardiac sympathetic support can deepen the fall.

sections.title: Microcirculation, Starling forces, lymph and edema

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Diffusion dominates exchange of gases and many small solutes. Lipid-soluble substances cross endothelial cell membranes readily, whereas hydrophilic solutes use clefts/fenestrae or transport pathways depending on the organ. Bulk fluid movement is governed by hydrostatic and oncotic forces plus filtration coefficient and barrier properties. It should not be confused with molecular diffusion.

The conventional Starling expression is Jv = Kf[(Pc - Pi) - σ(πc - πi)]. Capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes outward filtration, interstitial pressure opposes it when positive, plasma oncotic pressure opposes filtration and interstitial oncotic pressure favors it. The reflection coefficient describes restriction of protein movement. In glycocalyx-aware physiology, the effective oncotic gradient is across the endothelial surface layer and subglycocalyx space. Do not assume every systemic capillary routinely reabsorbs large amounts of fluid along its venous end; lymphatic return is essential.

blocks.title: Conventional course model versus research refinement
blocks.text: The conventional equation is the course/book calculation model. The glycocalyx and mainly outward steady-state exchange qualification is additionally supported by Levick and Michel, Microvascular fluid exchange and the revised Starling principle (2010), DOI 10.1093/cvr/cvq062, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20200043/. Transient absorption and specialized absorbing beds remain possible; this is not a claim that reabsorption never occurs.

rows: Higher permeability/Kf or lower protein reflection
Greater extracellular volume and capillary pressure

blocks.text: Initial lymphatic endothelial overlaps function as entry flaps anchored to surrounding tissue. Collecting lymphatics have valves and smooth muscle, assisted by skeletal and respiratory movement. Lymph returns filtered protein as well as water. Increased lymph flow, interstitial pressure changes and protein washout can buffer edema until their capacity is exceeded.

blocks.question: Why can edema occur without an elevated arterial pressure?
blocks.answer: Venous pressure, low plasma protein, increased permeability or impaired lymph drainage can each shift fluid balance. Arterial pressure is only one upstream determinant of capillary filtration.

sections.title: Local blood-flow control, autoregulation and special circuits

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Active hyperemia is increased flow during increased tissue metabolism. Reactive hyperemia is transient excess flow after release of occlusion because vasodilator metabolites and oxygen debt accumulated during ischemia. Myogenic autoregulation responds to increased vessel stretch with contraction, stabilizing flow despite a changed perfusion pressure. Metabolic autoregulation links local flow to nutrient demand and waste accumulation. These mechanisms interact and have finite operating ranges.

Reduced local oxygen and increased CO2/H+, K+, adenosine and other metabolites generally dilate systemic tissue resistance vessels. Endothelial shear stress stimulates nitric oxide, which activates smooth-muscle cGMP and relaxation. Endothelin is a potent constrictor. Histamine and bradykinin can promote dilation and increased permeability. Epinephrine is receptor- and dose-dependent: beta-2 effects can dilate some beds while alpha effects constrict others. It must not be classified as universally vasoconstricting.

The brain receives roughly 14% of a typical resting output in the lecture/Guyton illustration, not the 40% ASR wording. Cerebral flow responds strongly to CO2/H+. Coronary flow follows myocardial metabolism. Renal flow has filtration-related requirements rather than simply matching oxygen use. Hepatic flow is dual, from portal vein and hepatic artery. Pulmonary vessels constrict with alveolar hypoxia, the important opposite response that redistributes flow away from poorly ventilated lung units.

blocks.question: A cuff briefly stops forearm flow; release gives a transient overshoot. Why is this not the same as active hyperemia?
blocks.answer: It is reactive hyperemia caused by the preceding interruption of perfusion and accumulated local metabolic signals. Active hyperemia is driven by increased ongoing tissue activity even without prior occlusion.

sections.title: Baroreceptors, chemoreceptors and central pressure regulation

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors sense stretch. Increased pressure increases afferent firing through Hering/glossopharyngeal and vagal pathways to the nucleus tractus solitarius. The integrated response decreases sympathetic tone and increases cardiac vagal activity, reducing rate, contractility and vascular resistance. A fall in pressure produces the opposite response. Rapid changes strongly influence firing. Baroreceptors buffer acute changes and can reset with sustained pressure changes.

Carotid and aortic bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors sensing oxygen, CO2 and H+. Their contribution to ventilation and circulation depends on the context, especially whether breathing is allowed to change. In a low-perfusion state they can contribute sympathetic vasoconstriction. The slide statement that a generic chemoreflex simply lowers pressure should not replace this integrated account. Carotid sinus is a pressure sensor and carotid body a chemical sensor despite their proximity.

CNS ischemic responses can strongly activate sympathetic output when medullary perfusion becomes critically low. Raised intracranial pressure can elicit a Cushing response with increased systemic pressure and reflex bradycardia. Vasovagal syncope instead combines inappropriate vasodilation with reduced heart rate, lowering cerebral perfusion. Sympathetic tone is not switched off everywhere during normal rest, and an anatomic diagram of several medullary groups does not mean each group is an isolated on/off switch.

blocks.question: Why does standing normally cause a rapid increase in heart rate before renal compensation could act?
blocks.answer: Venous pooling reduces central filling and arterial stretch at baroreceptors. Reduced afferent firing rapidly increases sympathetic and reduces vagal cardiac activity. Renal volume regulation acts over a longer timescale.

sections.title: Renal-body fluid feedback and hormonal pressure control

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Long-term pressure control depends strongly on sodium and water balance. Pressure natriuresis and diuresis increase salt/water excretion when renal perfusion pressure rises, reducing extracellular volume, venous return and ultimately output. The relation can shift with renal disease, sympathetic input and hormones. A single elevated reading does not establish a chronic set point or identify its mechanism.

Reduced renal perfusion, lower macula-densa salt delivery and beta-1 sympathetic drive stimulate renin. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen, and ACE generates angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts resistance vessels and stimulates aldosterone, thirst and vasopressin-related water conservation. Aldosterone increases distal sodium retention. Natriuretic peptides oppose volume expansion by promoting natriuresis and modulating renal/vascular function. Vasopressin increases collecting-duct water permeability and, at sufficiently high concentrations, can constrict vessels.

Do not treat hypertension as a permanent rise in resistance alone. Acute vasoconstriction can raise pressure, but chronic behavior depends on interaction with renal excretion and volume. Conversely, compensatory fluid retention after pump failure can restore some output while worsening congestion. Mechanistic questions often ask whether an intervention changes resistance, volume, contractility or more than one variable.

blocks.question: Why does an acute fall in pressure activate both a rapid neural response and slower renin-angiotensin/volume responses?
blocks.answer: The neural response rapidly redistributes blood and supports pressure, while endocrine and renal mechanisms conserve sodium/water to restore filling. Their timescales and controlled variables differ, so one does not replace the other.

sections.title: Coronary perfusion, exercise and oxygen demand

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Left ventricular coronary flow is strongly reduced during systole by compression of intramyocardial vessels, especially in subendocardial layers, and is greatest during diastole. Right ventricular flow is less suppressed because RV systolic pressure is lower. Coronary perfusion pressure is often approximated by aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure. Tachycardia both increases oxygen demand and shortens diastolic perfusion time.

Myocardium extracts a high fraction of delivered oxygen at rest. Increased demand therefore requires increased coronary flow more than a large extraction reserve. Increased heart rate, contractility and wall stress raise oxygen consumption. With a thin-wall model, tension rises with pressure and radius, while increased wall thickness lowers stress. Dilated ventricles can require more oxygen for the same external work. This links Laplace reasoning to ischemia and failure.

Dynamic exercise combines increased sympathetic cardiac drive, increased venous return and metabolic vasodilation in active muscle. Splanchnic/renal vasoconstriction and venoconstriction help redistribute flow, while skeletal muscle pump and respiration assist return. Local metabolic dilation in working muscle can override sympathetic constriction. Total peripheral resistance may decrease even while systolic pressure and cardiac output rise. A sustained contraction can mechanically compress muscle vessels, with increased flow during relaxation.

blocks.question: Why is subendocardium particularly vulnerable when tachycardia coexists with high LV filling pressure?
blocks.answer: Tachycardia shortens diastole, while high LV end-diastolic pressure reduces the coronary driving gradient. Subendocardial vessels already undergo strong systolic compression, so their perfusion reserve is limited.

sections.title: Shock, heart failure and valve lesions: integrated physiology

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Shock is inadequate effective tissue perfusion, not simply a low cuff pressure. Hypovolemic shock reduces circulating volume and preload. Cardiogenic shock reflects inadequate pump function. Obstructive shock impedes filling or outflow, as in tamponade or major pulmonary vascular obstruction. Distributive shock lowers effective vascular tone and can involve maldistributed flow. The early hemodynamic pattern depends on cause and stage.

Hemorrhage reduces systemic filling pressure and venous return. Baroreflex activation causes tachycardia, increased sympathetic contractility and vasoconstriction, with cold skin and reduced renal flow in a typical compensated pattern. Renin-angiotensin, vasopressin and fluid shifts contribute later. Do not memorize the lecture assertion that a fixed percentage of bleeding inevitably causes irreversible death or that contractility never increases. Outcome depends on rate, severity, compensation and treatment.

rows: LV pressure overload and increased afterload
Elevated LA/pulmonary venous pressure, impaired LV filling
Systolic LV-to-LA backflow, LA/LV volume load

blocks.text: Left-sided failure raises pulmonary venous pressure and can produce pulmonary edema. Right-sided failure raises systemic venous pressure and can produce peripheral edema/hepatic congestion. Reduced EF is one failure phenotype; stiff ventricles can fail despite preserved EF. S3 can reflect rapid filling of a volume-loaded ventricle, while S4 reflects atrial contraction against reduced ventricular compliance. These are physiologic associations, not sufficient diagnostic criteria alone.

blocks.question: Why can tamponade resemble right-sided failure with neck-vein distension but involve neither an intrinsic RV muscle defect nor a blocked tricuspid valve?
blocks.answer: External pericardial pressure impedes diastolic filling. Upstream venous pressure rises while effective forward output falls. The limiting structure is the pericardial enclosure.

sections.title: Preserved ejection fraction, valve geometry and shock mechanisms

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Ejection fraction is a fraction, not a flow. With EF 60%, EDV 120 mL gives SV 72 mL, whereas EDV 70 mL gives SV 42 mL. At 80/min their outputs are 5.76 and 3.36 L/min. A stiff small ventricle may therefore empty a normal fraction yet provide inadequate stroke volume at high filling pressure. Resting output can be maintained through elevated filling pressure while exercise reserve remains poor. Further salt/water retention eventually raises congestion more than useful output.

Aortic stenosis imposes pressure overload; LV pressure must exceed aortic pressure sufficiently to drive flow across the narrowed orifice. Regurgitation imposes a volume load and makes total ejection larger than effective forward output. If total ejection is 160 mL and regurgitation is 100 mL, forward SV is only 60 mL; at 75/min forward output is 4.5 L/min. Functional mitral regurgitation can arise from annular dilation, papillary displacement and leaflet tethering without a primary leaflet tear. S4 requires organized atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, so atrial fibrillation can abolish the sound without curing stiffness.

Shock concerns inadequate tissue perfusion relative to need. Compensatory vasoconstriction may preserve arterial pressure better than output, masking regional underperfusion. Hemorrhage lowers stressed volume; venodilation can mimic its filling-pressure effect without identical blood loss. Plasma loss can increase hematocrit/viscosity while reducing circulating volume. Histamine-mediated venodilation plus capillary leak combines increased capacity with actual intravascular depletion.

In septic/distributive shock, low systemic resistance and normal or high total output do not prove adequate microvascular oxygen delivery. Heterogeneous flow, leakage, increased demand and microthrombi can coexist. Widespread intravascular coagulation may obstruct microvessels while consuming platelets/coagulation factors and causing bleeding elsewhere. Ischemic endothelial injury increases permeability, which worsens circulating volume and perfusion: a positive-feedback loop. Late mitochondrial injury and loss of high-energy reserves mean transiently restored pressure does not instantly reverse cellular damage. This is a mechanism of severe illness, not a bedside rule for declaring treatment futile.

blocks.question: Why is high cardiac output compatible with septic shock while low output is typical in major hemorrhage?
blocks.answer: Sepsis can lower resistance and raise metabolic demand while distributing flow inadequately at the microvascular level. Hemorrhage usually limits filling and output directly. The label shock refers to the tissue-perfusion problem, not one obligatory cardiac-output value.

sections.title: ECG calibration, lead geometry and a systematic interpretation

sources.title: ECG  & vectorial analysis with narration - Copy — Readable copy.pptx
Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: An ECG records differences in extracellular electrical potential. A depolarization wave moving toward a positive electrode produces an upward deflection; repolarization has opposite electrical polarity. A lead is a viewing axis and is not identical to an electrode. Twelve conventional leads use ten electrodes. Limb lead I is LA-RA, II is LL-RA and III is LL-LA, so II = I + III. Augmented leads and precordial leads provide additional views.

Before diagnosing, confirm patient/context, artifact, speed, gain and lead placement. Then assess rate, regularity, P-wave behavior, P-QRS relationship, PR, QRS width, axis, R-wave progression and ST-T changes. At 25 mm/s a regular rate is 300 divided by large squares between R waves or 1500 divided by small squares. For an irregular rhythm, count QRS complexes in a known time interval and scale to one minute. A short snapshot can misrepresent variability.

V1 and V2 lie in the fourth intercostal spaces at right/left sternal borders. V4 is fifth intercostal space at left midclavicular line. V3 lies between V2 and V4. V5 and V6 are horizontally level with V4 at anterior and midaxillary lines. The transcript phrase putting V6 in the sixth intercostal space is erroneous. Chest leads should not be moved upward to follow breast contour.

blocks.question: A trace is too compressed horizontally to distinguish atrial activity during tachycardia. Which adjustment improves temporal separation, and what must then change in rate calculation?
blocks.answer: Increasing paper speed, for example from 25 to 50 mm/s, spreads events horizontally. Each small square then represents 0.02 rather than 0.04 s. Gain changes vertical amplitude, not horizontal time.

blocks.caption: Distinguish waves, segments and intervals; atrial and ventricular timing is not the same as mechanical pressure.

sections.title: Cardiac axis and vector interpretation

sources.title: ECG  & vectorial analysis with narration - Copy — Readable copy.pptx
Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: The frontal QRS axis reflects the net ventricular depolarization vector. Lead I points to 0 degrees, II to +60, aVF to +90, III to +120, aVL to -30 and aVR to -150. An isoelectric/equiphasic QRS suggests the mean vector is approximately perpendicular to that lead. There are always two opposite perpendicular possibilities; polarity in another lead selects the correct one.

For an equiphasic aVR, candidate directions are about -60 and +120 degrees. Positive lead I and negative inferior leads favor -60, while negative I and positive inferior leads favor +120. Do not infer one number from aVR alone. The common adult normal range is approximately -30 to +90 degrees, with variation by age, body habitus and reference. Positive I and negative aVF can still be normal if lead II is positive; this distinguishes a mildly leftward normal axis from more definite left-axis deviation.

rows: Still inspect morphology and clinical setting
Not every such tracing is pathological LAD
Consider age, RV load, conduction or lead reversal
Check technical errors and ventricular rhythms

blocks.text: An abnormal axis can reflect ventricular mass, conduction sequence, infarcted tissue or lead misplacement. QRS width helps distinguish a conduction abnormality from an isolated shift in mean direction. Ventricular repolarization often gives a positive T wave in the same lead as a positive QRS because repolarization usually propagates in the opposite spatial direction and has opposite electrical polarity.

blocks.question: Why is a positive T wave not proof that repolarization travels in the same direction as depolarization?
blocks.answer: Repolarization reverses the sign of the electrical wave. A spatial direction opposite to depolarization can therefore produce the same positive surface deflection.

blocks.text: PR is normally about 0.12-0.20 s in adult teaching examples. A QRS of at least 0.12 s is wide. QT depends on rate, so QTc interpretation requires a correction method and clinical context. ST elevation, depression or T inversion can indicate ischemia but have alternative causes; compare contiguous leads, reciprocal changes, morphology and timing. A single labeled internet example is not a universal template. Anatomical territories are broadly inferior II/III/aVF, high lateral I/aVL, and precordial septal/anterior/lateral views, with overlapping supply.

blocks.question: A regular ventricular rate near 150/min appears without obvious P waves. Why should atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction remain a possibility?
blocks.answer: One flutter wave may be buried in each QRS/T cycle. A longer strip and leads that display atrial activity better can reveal organized atrial activity around twice the ventricular rate. Rate alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

sections.title: Pacemaker competition, reentry and vector calculations

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: The fastest effective pacemaker normally repeatedly resets subsidiary pacemakers. After sinus-to-ventricle conduction fails, a slower escape rhythm may take time to emerge. Acetylcholine increases nodal K+ conductance and suppresses pacemaker/Ca2+ currents, hyperpolarizing cells and delaying threshold. Slower Purkinje/ventricular propagation broadens QRS and reduces synchrony, whereas AV-nodal delay mainly alters the atrial-to-ventricular interval.

Reentry requires an excitable pathway, suitable unidirectional block and sufficient time for tissue ahead of a returning wave to recover. Circuit transit time is path length divided by conduction speed. Equivalently, refractory wavelength equals conduction speed times refractory period. A 12-cm circuit at 40 cm/s has a 0.30-s transit time; with a 0.25-s refractory period, recovery before return is possible. If speed falls to 25 cm/s and refractory period rises to 0.36 s, wavelength is still only 9 cm, below circuit length. Prolonging refractoriness therefore does not automatically terminate reentry if conduction changes too.

A surface lead measures projection, not the full cardiac vector magnitude. A 2-mV vector at +60 degrees projects as 2 cos60 = +1 mV in lead I. Calibration is equally essential: 8 mm horizontally at 50 mm/s is 0.16 s; 8 mm vertically at 5 mm/mV is 1.6 mV. Low surface voltage may reflect altered myocardial activation, surrounding fluid or increased lung air and is not a direct one-to-one gauge of wall thickness. Atrial repolarization occurs but is usually obscured by QRS.

blocks.question: Lead I is positive, aVF negative and lead II negative. What is the geometric axis interval before assigning a clinical label?
blocks.answer: I+/aVF- places the vector between -90 and 0 degrees. Lead II is perpendicular at -30 degrees, so its negative projection narrows the interval to approximately -90 to -30 degrees. Borderline equiphasic tracings require allowance for measurement error.

sections.title: Erythrocytes, hematocrit and oxygen delivery

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Mature erythrocytes are flexible biconcave anucleate cells approximately 7-8 micrometers across. Their shape increases surface area relative to volume and permits capillary passage. Hemoglobin carries oxygen, carbonic anhydrase accelerates CO2 hydration, and hemoglobin buffers H+. Lacking mitochondria, RBCs obtain ATP through glycolysis rather than consuming the oxygen they transport. Membrane-cytoskeletal integrity and redox protection are essential for their survival.

Hematocrit is the packed RBC fraction of whole blood volume. Hemoglobin concentration, RBC count and hematocrit are related but are not interchangeable. Anemia is principally a reduction in hemoglobin/oxygen-carrying capacity relative to the appropriate reference population, not necessarily a reduction in the number of cells. Plasma volume changes can alter measured concentration without an equivalent immediate change in total red-cell mass.

rows: Hb concentration within packed RBC volume
mL O2/dL when Hb in g/dL, saturation as a fraction, PaO2 in mmHg

blocks.text: Oxygen delivery equals cardiac output times arterial oxygen content with unit conversion. A patient can have normal PaO2 but low oxygen content because hemoglobin is low. Increasing dissolved oxygen contributes little compared with hemoglobin-bound oxygen under ordinary conditions. Interpret oxygen pressure, saturation and content as distinct quantities.

blocks.question: Why can a severely anemic patient have a normal pulse-oximeter percentage?
blocks.answer: The percentage reports the fraction of available hemoglobin binding sites occupied, not how much hemoglobin is present. Normal saturation with low Hb can still mean low total arterial oxygen content.

sections.title: Erythropoiesis, iron and anemia mechanisms

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Low tissue oxygen availability increases renal erythropoietin production through hypoxia-responsive signaling. EPO promotes erythroid progenitor survival and differentiation in marrow. The series proceeds through proerythroblast, basophilic, polychromatophilic and orthochromatic erythroblast stages, nuclear extrusion, reticulocyte and mature RBC. Cell size and nuclear size fall while hemoglobin accumulates. Reticulocytes retain residual RNA and indicate recent marrow output, but the percentage must be interpreted relative to the anemia and maturation time.

Vitamin B12 and folate support DNA synthesis, so deficiency produces ineffective, megaloblastic erythropoiesis. Iron deficiency limits heme synthesis and commonly produces microcytic hypochromic cells. Chronic blood loss can deplete iron, while acute blood loss is initially normocytic and may not immediately lower concentration before fluid redistribution. Renal failure can reduce EPO, marrow failure can impair multiple cell lines, and hemolysis increases red-cell destruction.

Iron is absorbed mainly in the proximal small intestine, circulates bound to transferrin and is stored principally in ferritin, with hemosiderin in larger stores. Hepcidin reduces ferroportin-mediated iron export from enterocytes and macrophages, restricting availability. Senescent RBCs are removed mainly by macrophages, especially in spleen/liver/marrow; iron is recycled and heme is converted toward bilirubin. Mature RBC life is approximately 120 days. Secondary erythrocytosis can be hypoxia-driven, whereas a myeloproliferative process is not the same adaptive mechanism.

blocks.caption: Follow the decrease in size, chromatin condensation, changing cytoplasmic staining and nuclear loss across erythroid maturation.

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Tissue-resident macrophages can respond immediately to injury. Neutrophils are recruited from blood, while later monocyte-derived macrophages and increased marrow production sustain responses. Selectin-mediated rolling, chemokine activation, integrin-mediated firm adhesion and transendothelial migration are sequentially different events. The principal site of routine inflammatory leukocyte exit is the postcapillary venule. Opsonins such as IgG and C3b improve phagocytosis. NADPH oxidase generates superoxide; downstream peroxide and myeloperoxidase-dependent hypochlorous species contribute to killing.

Differential percentages require the total WBC concentration. If lymphocytes are 50% of 3,000 WBC/µL, their absolute count is 1,500/µL. A high relative fraction alone does not establish absolute lymphocytosis. Similarly, an apparently moderate neutrophil percentage can coexist with severe absolute neutropenia when total WBC count is very low. Reference intervals vary with age and laboratory.

blocks.question: Why can leukemia coexist with infection, anemia and bleeding despite a very high WBC count?
blocks.answer: A high count may consist of dysfunctional/clonal cells and can displace normal marrow production. Effective host defense, erythropoiesis and platelet production can therefore be impaired rather than improved.

sections.title: Primary hemostasis and platelet biology

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Hemostasis begins with local vasoconstriction and a platelet response, then a fibrin network stabilizes the plug. Platelets are anucleate cytoplasmic fragments of megakaryocytes. Their cytoskeleton changes shape during activation, granules release mediators, and membrane phospholipids provide a reaction surface for coagulation complexes. Primary and secondary hemostasis interact; they are not isolated systems reserved exclusively for small versus large vessels.

Exposed collagen and von Willebrand factor support platelet adhesion, particularly through GPIb-vWF interaction. Activation releases ADP and produces thromboxane A2, recruiting more platelets. Activated GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen to bridge platelets in aggregation. Alpha granules contain proteins such as vWF and growth factors; dense granules contain ADP/ATP, calcium and serotonin. Cytoskeletal contraction contributes to clot retraction. The liver is a major source of thrombopoietin.

rows: Mucocutaneous bleeding, petechiae or prolonged bleeding from small injuries

Adhesion and aggregation are not interchangeable

blocks.title: Lifespan versus half-life
blocks.text: The lecture gives an approximately 8-12 day survival figure but labels it half-life. Treat it as an approximate platelet lifespan statement, not a rigorously defined elimination half-life.

sections.title: Coagulation cascade, anticoagulants and fibrinolysis

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: Tissue factor with factor VIIa initiates coagulation after injury. The classic intrinsic scheme uses XII, XI, IX and VIII; the extrinsic route is tissue factor/VII. They converge on factor X. Xa with Va, calcium and a phospholipid surface forms prothrombinase, generating thrombin from prothrombin. Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, activates factor XIII to cross-link it and amplifies activation of platelets and several cofactors. The cell-based in-vivo process is more integrated than two independent linear tubes.

rows: Cofactors, not the same proteases as activated IX or X
II, VII, IX, X plus proteins C and S
Inhibits thrombin and activated coagulation proteases; enhanced by heparin
Activated protein C with S inactivates Va and VIIIa
tPA activates plasminogen; plasmin degrades fibrin
PT emphasizes extrinsic/common; aPTT intrinsic/common pathways

blocks.text: Serum is the liquid remaining after clotting and differs from plasma by consumption/removal of fibrinogen and changes in several coagulation proteins. Most clotting proteins are synthesized in liver, but the slide statement that all except tissue factor come from hepatocytes is too broad: endothelial cells are important for vWF and factor VIII. Vitamin K supports gamma-carboxylation needed for calcium-dependent membrane binding. Fibrinolysis is regulated continuously and should not be imagined as beginning only a fixed number of days after injury.

blocks.question: Why can an isolated factor XIII deficiency produce bleeding while routine PT and aPTT remain normal?
blocks.answer: Those tests detect formation of the initial fibrin clot. Factor XIII stabilizes fibrin by cross-linking after that endpoint, so defective clot stability may not prolong those screening times.

sections.title: ABO, Rh and transfusion concepts

sources.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (2026).pdf

blocks.text: ABO antigens are carbohydrate determinants on RBC surfaces. Plasma commonly contains antibodies against the absent A/B antigen, with important age and immune-history exceptions. A recipient receiving incompatible donor RBCs can develop antibody-mediated agglutination and hemolysis. RBC and plasma compatibility run in different directions because one product supplies cells and the other supplies antibodies.

Rh D is a major RBC protein antigen. Anti-D generally follows exposure rather than being naturally present in an unsensitized person. Maternal IgG can cross the placenta and damage fetal RBCs if fetal antigen is incompatible with maternal sensitization. Distinguish immune hemolysis from an intrinsic membrane or hemoglobin defect. The phrase universal donor is context-dependent: component type, Rh, minor antigens and crossmatching remain important.

blocks.question: Why does the blood group that is convenient for emergency RBC donation not automatically make the best universal plasma donor?
blocks.answer: RBC compatibility is governed mainly by donor cell antigens meeting recipient antibodies. Plasma compatibility depends on donor antibodies encountering recipient RBC antigens, reversing the ABO logic.
